sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content: • **Geopolitical Ambition**: Rana Sanga aimed to establish a Rajput hegemony over North India, viewing Babur as a temporary invader like Timur. • **Babur's Justification**: Babur accused Sanga of breaking a diplomatic agreement (alleged promise to attack Ibrahim Lodi from the south). • **Military Asymmetry**: The conflict was a clash between traditional Rajput cavalry-based warfare and the **Tulugma** (flanking) and **Araba** (cart-wagon) tactics of the Mughals. • **Psychological Warfare**: Babur declared the war a **Jihad** against infidels to boost the morale of his exhausted troops, who were terrified of the Rajput reputation.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content: • **Artillery Integration**: First major use of field artillery in North India. • **Religious Mobilization**: Use of 'Jihad' rhetoric to unify a diverse, multi-ethnic army.

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content: • **Key Challenges**: High desertion rates among Mughal troops due to fear of Rajput valor. • **Solutions**: Babur's public renunciation of wine and the abolition of the Tamgha tax to demonstrate commitment to Islamic law.

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content: • **Memory Acronym**: 'P-K-C-G' (Panipat, Khanwa, Chanderi, Ghagra). • **Decoded Meaning**: Chronological order of Babur's major battles (1526, 1527, 1528, 1529).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often confuses the 'Battle of Khanwa' with the 'Battle of Haldighati'. Khanwa was Babur vs. Sanga (1527); Haldighati was Akbar vs. Maharana Pratap (1576).
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Military Revolution' to describe the introduction of gunpowder and field artillery in the Indian subcontinent by Babur.

keyTakeaways: The Battle of Khanwa was more significant than Panipat in securing the Mughal Empire as it defeated the strongest indigenous power of the time.
The victory established the superiority of gunpowder-based warfare over traditional cavalry charges.
Babur's success was a combination of superior technology, tactical flexibility, and astute psychological management of his troops.
